identity.title: alpha-Halogenated Curcumins Enhance the Binding Affinity and Induced Structural Alterations to Amyloid-beta Protein in Alzheimer's Disease.

content.abstract: Amyloid-beta (Abeta) aggregation and associated structural changes are central features of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. In this study, we investigated the binding of alpha-halogenated curcumins, alpha-bromocurcumin and alpha-chlorocurcumin, to Abeta(1-42) and examined their effects on the peptide secondary structure using fluorescence spectroscopy and circular dichroism (CD). Both alpha-halogenated curcumins interacted with Abeta(1-42), but their binding properties differed from those of the parent curcumin. alpha-Chlorocurcumin exhibited a higher binding affinity for Abeta(1-42) than curcumin, whereas alpha-bromocurcumin showed comparatively weaker binding. Temperature-dependent binding studies revealed that the association of alpha-halogenated curcumins with Abeta(1-42) was influenced by temperature, with reduced binding affinity at higher temperatures. Thermodynamic analysis demonstrated favorable free-energy changes for the interactions and revealed that alpha-halogenation altered the relative enthalpic and entropic contributions to Abeta(1-42) binding. CD analysis further showed that binding of the curcumin altered the secondary structure of Abeta(1-42). These structural changes were more pronounced in the presence of the alpha-halogenated derivatives, indicating that halogen substitution influences the interaction and conformational response of Abeta(1-42). Molecular docking analysis provided additional insight into the possible binding modes and predicted intermolecular contacts between the alpha-halogenated curcumin and Abeta(1-42). Overall, the findings demonstrate that alpha-halogenation modulates the binding and structural effects of curcumin derivatives on Abeta(1-42), with alpha-chlorocurcumin exhibiting particularly favorable binding characteristics. These findings provide a basis for further investigation of alpha-halogenated curcumins as potential modulators of Abeta-related molecular processes associated with AD.
